Ingest Schedule R related organisations as observed names and addresses

Source: R/md-ingest-schedr.R
md_ingest_schedr.Rd

The same files md_ingest_relations() reads for its affiliate pairs also carry the related organisation's name and address, written by the filer. That makes Schedule R Part II a second (name, address) -> EIN source of the same kind as Schedule I, and reading only the EIN pair discards it.

Usage

md_ingest_schedr(
  version = "v2_2",
  con = NULL,
  min_corroborators = 1L,
  guard = TRUE
)

Arguments

version

Pinned efile_related version.

con

A connection from md_db().

min_corroborators

Minimum distinct filers. Defaults to 1; see above for how corroboration actually distributes here.

guard

Run md_guard_observed() on the loaded rows (see md_ingest_schedi()). A filer listing itself as a related organisation under a different name is the own-EIN case here.

Value

Row counts, invisibly.

How this differs from Schedule I

Both are third parties writing about an EIN, so both are observed (section 3a). The expectation going in was that Schedule R would be the weaker of the two on corroboration - a related organisation is disclosed only by its own affiliates, of which there might be one or two, where a Schedule I recipient is written about by whoever happened to fund it.

Measured, that is wrong, and in the useful direction. Schedule R is the better corroborated source of the pair:


  distinct filers    schedi          schedr
  1                  1,339,769 77.8
  2-4                  276,766 16.1
  5-19                  95,735  5.6
  20+                   10,534  0.6

Fewer single-filer rows, and eight times the share at twenty or more. Group structure is why: a national organisation with hundreds of chapters is disclosed by every one of them, so the very entities most likely to be confused with their affiliates are the ones carrying the most corroboration.

The practical consequence is the opposite of what was assumed - a shared min_corroborators floor costs less here than on Schedule I, not more.

The near-identical-name hazard

Schedule R names are systematically related to the filer's, since an organisation and its supporting foundation usually share a stem. That is exactly the condition section 10 warns produces false matches.

What makes it safe is that every row carries the disclosed EIN. The name attaches to the organisation it names rather than to the filer, which is the difference between recording an affiliate's name as an alias of itself - fine, and the point - and as an alias of its parent, which section 10 forbids.
